data.title: Trump, Xi and Putin Convene First-Ever Summit as World Order Shifts — WSJ
data.description:
By Vera Bergengruen, Jonathan Cheng and Marianne LeVine

SHENZHEN, China — President Trump met with Chinese leader Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin in this southern Chinese city on Thursday, in an unprecedented show of unity among the stewards of the world's three largest nuclear arsenals.

The first-ever gathering of the American, Chinese and Russian leaders was a further sign of the end of a unipolar world order dominated by the U.S. — and suggested that what might replace it is a more uncertain, and unsettled, reality.

"We are really making history," Trump said as the three leaders opened the 90-minute meeting, sitting around a large, round wooden table under a towering Chinese landscape painting. "No problems were ever solved under the old school, refusing to talk about them."

The three remain divided by their competing ambitions and sharply conflicting visions of what a new world order should look like.

Russia and the U.S. are bogged down in wars, while Beijing faces mounting economic problems and is deeply reluctant to take on the kind of global leadership role historically played by the U.S.

What the three leaders do share is a desire to be able to operate without constraints in their respective spheres.

Putin wants Washington to stay out of his way in Ukraine. Xi wants the U.S. to accept his claim that self-ruled Taiwan belongs to China. And Trump has made pushing Chinese and Russian influence out of the Western Hemisphere a central element of his so-called "Donroe Doctrine" to reassert U.S. dominance in the region.

There was little indication that progress could be made on the major issues they brought to the table: the wars in Ukraine and Iran and the proliferation of nuclear weapons.

But for the three men in the spotlight, just sitting down together was the point.

The three leaders met at Kylin Villa, a secluded government guesthouse at the foot of the hills of Shenzhen that has hosted China's political elite and foreign dignitaries.

Going into the meeting, Trump embraced the historic gathering to promote an image of himself as a global peacemaker alongside two autocrats whom he has long admired.

"All my life I read you'd never want to have Russia and China team up. That was like 101 in politics or in warfare," Trump said in a Fox News interview before the meeting. "They both like Trump. Now, what happens after me? That I can't tell you."

He left Washington with his party reeling from its midterm defeats, eager to use his final two years in office to cement his legacy on the world stage. "We have a chance to accomplish a lot," he said as he departed for Asia.

Trump headed first to a meeting of Southeast Asian leaders in Manila and then to Shenzhen for the annual APEC gathering of Asia-Pacific leaders, hosted this year by China.

When Trump landed Wednesday in Shenzhen, Xi welcomed him with the pomp Trump relishes, personally greeting him on the tarmac, a first by a Chinese president, and arranging a colorful military flyover — just as Trump did for Xi on his arrival in the U.S. in September.

Trump offered little indication of what he hoped to accomplish with Xi and Putin in Shenzhen, beyond opening talks on nuclear arms control. U.S. officials played down any prospects of a breakthrough.

Trump acknowledged in the Fox News interview that reaching an agreement on reducing nuclear arsenals would be challenging.

"When they look at me and they say, 'OK we'll do it, but will you reduce your nuclear weapons by 2,000 weapons?'...It's a hard thing to do," Trump said. "For me, it's a hard thing. And it's probably hard for them to do also."

The New Strategic Arms Reduction Treaty, or New START, the last treaty limiting Washington and Moscow's strategic nuclear arsenals, expired earlier this year. Trump has pushed for a broader agreement that would include China, whose rapid rise as a nuclear power brings new complications to any denuclearization effort.

Trump had also repeatedly floated the prospect that his trip to Asia would include a meeting with North Korean leader Kim Jong Un, who is building his own nuclear arsenal. By the time the trilateral meeting adjourned there was no sign that a Trump-Kim session would materialize.

For Putin, the gathering marked a remarkable diplomatic comeback nearly five years after his invasion of Ukraine made him an international pariah.

"He's my friend," Trump said after greeting Putin for a two-way meeting earlier in the day. "We knew each other for a long time, and I think a lot of wonderful things can come out of this."

Trump later said he and Putin had a lengthy discussion on Ukraine, suggesting there had been progress without offering specifics. "I think things are happening," he said.

The Russian leader had first proposed a trilateral summit alongside the APEC meetings as a venue to discuss ending the Ukraine war.

In the end, Putin's place at the sit-down with the leaders of the world's two largest economies underscored the limits of Western efforts to isolate him.

"Our three nations are united not only by the status of victors in the Second World War but mainly by our responsibility for maintaining international peace," Putin said at the meeting.

Xi, while playing host, has in some ways been the reluctant party among the three. Beijing has long said that it doesn't belong in arms-control talks, saying its arsenal is dwarfed by those of Washington and Moscow.

But Xi benefits just by being there. The meeting places the Chinese leader on an equal footing, for the third time this year, with the U.S. president, while standing alongside a close partner in Putin over whom he holds an overwhelming advantage.

"What Xi gains from this trilateral meeting is the chance to look like the pivot player in international politics, convening this would-be 'G3' on Chinese soil and sitting alongside his closest partner on the world stage, Putin, to negotiate with a remarkably friendly American president," said Julian Gewirtz, a China-focused official in the Biden-era National Security Council.

As Trump met with Xi ahead of the trilateral, he framed his "very special relationship" with the Chinese leader as the cornerstone of U.S.-China stability.

"As long as you and I are in charge of things, we'll never have a problem," Trump said as he met with Xi. "We're never gonna have a problem."

Write to Vera Bergengruen at vera.bergengruen@wsj.com, Jonathan Cheng at Jonathan.Cheng@wsj.com and Marianne LeVine at marianne.levine@wsj.com

Commentary3

The Company’s NAV declined by 18.09% in October, following similar losses in the previous

month. These results were slightly behind both developed and junior uranium miners.

October saw a notable acceleration in nuclear demand signaling, with a series of hyperscaler

commitments and government-backed investments reinforcing the fundamental backdrop for

uranium, which we’ve seen underpinned by ongoing policy momentum, energy security concerns,

reliable carbon-free power, and hyperscalers’ growing power demand for data centers. Notably,

Google and Constellation Energy announced a 20-year power purchase agreement covering 890

MW of nuclear capacity across 11 reactors, representing more than $4.3Bn of investment by

Constellation. Amazon followed with a separate partnership with AEP and X-Energy to explore a

960 MW advanced nuclear project in Indiana, utilizing 12 SMRs with Amazon as the long-term

power offtaker. The increased frequency of announcements further demonstrates that hyperscaler

demand is moving beyond exploratory interest towards long-term commitments to nuclear

generation. Government support also continued to build, with the DOE offering Constellation up to

$5Bn in conditional loan financing to modernize its nuclear fleet. In comparison, Vistra secured a

separate commitment of up to $4.2Bn for upgrades at three plants, preserving nearly 4 GW of

baseload capacity and adding 433 MW of capacity. Internationally, Slovakia signed a pre-

engineering contract with Westinghouse as a formal step toward a new 1200 MW state-owned

reactor estimated at €15Bn, while Indonesia formally incorporated a 7 GW nuclear target into its

national energy strategy.

Alongside the improving demand outlook, supply security and the availability of future production

remain key concerns for the market. A significant supply-side development came from

Kazakhstan, where Kazatomprom shareholders rejected a uranium supply contract with Uranium

One, part of Russia’s Rosatom, while simultaneously approving a supply agreement with China’s

SNURDC. The decision highlights the geopolitical complexity surrounding uranium supply,

particularly as Kazakhstan accounts for approximately 40% of global production and Western

utilities seek diversification. More broadly, the uranium market remains structurally tight, with

primary mine production falling short of reactor requirements and the deficit increasingly met

through secondary sources, which are diminishing. Looking further ahead, supply challenges

become more pronounced as several of the industry’s largest mines, including major assets

operated by Kazatomprom and Cameco, are expected to deplete in the 2030s, even after planned

life extensions. At the same time, the lowest-cost sources of supply are moving up the cost curve,

increasing the incentive price required to bring new production online.

Still, elevated long-term contract prices and signs of accelerating utility contracting support

ongoing tightness in the uranium market and a constructive medium-term price outlook. The

Athabasca Basin remains a critical source of future supply growth, as companies continue to

advance projects. Notably, NexGen’s Rook I project and Denison’s Phoenix Project continue

construction, with targeted first production in 2030 and 2028, respectively. The spot uranium price

was up $3.10 to $92.55/lb over the month. The Company’s weighting is balanced between

producers and developers, with the latter expected to benefit from uncontracted volumes in a

rising long-term uranium price environment.

data.title: Gold recoups from 14-month low, tighter Fed outlook caps gains
data.description:
Key points:
  • Traders price in 90% chance of a 25-bp Fed hike in December
  • Raise rates by 50 bps in Dec or indicate quicker rate hikes ahead, Waller says
  • Elevated ETF positions could fuel gold liquidation- ANZ analysts

By Sherin Sans

Gold prices edged higher on Thursday as bargain hunting and shortcovering emerged after a sharp selloff that drove bullion to a 14-month low, although a firm dollar and mounting expectations of tighter US monetary policy capped gains.

Spot gold rose 0.2% to $3,730.61 per ounce by 0921 GMT, after touching its lowest level since September 2025 at $3,693.13 earlier in the session. US gold futures for December delivery fell 0.3% to $3,732.70.

"Today's move looks more like shortcovering and bargain hunting after a 3% drop to a 14-month low than a change in the bigger picture, which is a strong dollar, high yields and a hawkish leaning Fed," said Zain Vawda, market analyst at Audacity Capital.

"Interestingly, most of yesterday's drop happened before the minutes were even released, which tells you the market had already moved to price in a more hawkish Fed."

The US dollar index edged down on after a seven-session winning streak but remained underpinned by hawkish remarks from a Fed officials that reinforced the case for further rate hikes.

Bullion remained under pressure after Fed minutes showed policymakers saw rising inflation risks that may warrant a stronger policy response.

Adding to the hawkish message, Fed Governor Michael Barr said he would likely support tighter monetary policy in an economy still facing inflation pressures, while Governor Christopher Waller said the US central bank may need to respond more aggressively to rising prices.

Traders are pricing in a 90% chance of a 25-basis-point rate increase in December and nearly 11% probability of a larger 50-basis-point move, according to CME's FedWatch Tool.

Higher interest rates reduce the appeal of non-yielding bullion by raising its opportunity cost.

"Gold-backed ETF holdings remain elevated, which leaves room for liquidation as the risk of restrictive policy intensifies," analysts at ANZ said in a note.

Spot silver rose 0.1% to $45.07, platinum gained 0.9% to $1,382.85, and palladium climbed 0.8% to $955.83.

data.title: Tire Makers Face a Cloudy Near-Term Outlook — Market Talk
data.description: Shares in tire makers have had a strong run this year, but the near-term outlook is cloudier, Bernstein analysts write. "Cost inflation will hit hard in H1, pricing power is tougher than usual, and we see first signs of capacity growth exceeding demand in the premium segment," it says. Bernstein retains its outperform ratings on Continental and Pirelli stocks, where downside looks more limited, but downgrades Michelin shares to market-perform from outperform as 2027 consensus expectations are highest, valuation is most stretched, and strategic progress has disappointed. The bank lowers its Michelin price target to 32 euros from 36 euros and its Pirelli price target to 7.60 euros from 7.80 euros. It has an 82 euro target price for Continental. Michelin shares fall 0.7% to 31.98 euros, Pirelli shares fall 0.4% to 6.47 euros, and Continental shares rise 0.5% to 72.80 euros. (dominic.chopping@wsj.com)

data.title: Rubis Updates Terms For Proposed Transformation Into Public Company
data.description:
Rubis :

  • SAID ON WEDNESDAY IT UPDATED ITS TERMS FOR ITS PROPOSED TRANSFORMATION INTO A PUBLIC COMPANY

  • TO PROPOSE A COMPENSATION FOR THE GENERAL PARTNERS REDUCED TO APPROXIMATELY 11.4 MILLION NEW SHARES (PREVIOUSLY 12.7 MILLION SHARES)

  • COMPENSATION IS AT THE LOWER END OF THE RANGE OF 11.0% TO 12.3% OF THE SHARE CAPITAL BEFORE ISSUANCE SET BY LEDOUBLE

  • TO PROPOSE AN EXCEPTIONAL CASH DISTRIBUTION OF €1.50 PER EXISTING SHARE

  • SUPERVISORY BOARD ISSUED FAVOURABLE OPINION ON UPDATED TERMS
